sonnet.problem: The story card says a leper was 'unclean'. That gives away the answer 'clean' to the choice card right after it (card 2).
sonnet.rule: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

sonnet.problem: The card states as fact that the leper is 'sure Jesus CAN do it'. The text only has him say 'If You are willing, You can make me clean.' His inner certainty is a feeling stated as fact, not marked as Papa Dorin's guess.
sonnet.rule: He can guess at a feeling, marked as his own ("I think," "I bet"). Never as fact.

sonnet.problem: The question says as fact that the leper 'is sure' Jesus can make him clean and 'unsure' about willingness. The text doesn't say what he is sure or unsure of. Those are unmarked feelings and reasons added to the text.
sonnet.rule: He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

sonnet.problem: The story card only retells verse 42, which card 8 just asked about and revealed. It is a recap that adds nothing new.
The card ties the stern warning to Jesus silencing demons in Mark 1:34. Mark 1:43-44 give no reason for the warning, so the card links two passages in a way the texts do not state.
sonnet.rule: When he connects two passages, or explains what a law was for, he says only what the texts state.

sonnet.problem: The right answer 'As a testimony to them' uses 'them', which has no clear referent. The question names a single priest, so the baker cannot tell who 'them' is.
sonnet.rule: "He," "she" and "they" always point to someone the baker can tell.

sonnet.problem: The story card only retells that the man spreads the news. Card 15 just asked about and revealed exactly this, so the card repeats an answer already shown.
sonnet.rule: An answer shown on one card, right or wrong, isn't used again on a later card.

sonnet.problem: The wrong answer 'He finally gets some time alone' is a near-match for the right one. Verse 45 says Jesus stays out in solitary places, so a baker could argue it is true.
sonnet.rule: A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.
